Organizational Diagnosis · Nicole L. Turner

Most Organizations Skip the Diagnosis and Go Straight to the Prescription

Most organizations have no shortage of people capable of solving problems. What they often lack is a process for determining whether they are solving the right one.

According to research cited by Harvard Business School, 85 percent of executives believe their organizations are bad at diagnosing problems, and 87 percent believe that failure carries significant costs. Those numbers point to an interesting contradiction. Most organizations have no shortage of people capable of solving problems. What they often lack is a process for determining whether they are solving the right one.

I've used a medical analogy for years to describe the work I do with organizations.

You know something is going on with your body, but you don't know what it is. So you go to the doctor. The doctor doesn't hand you a prescription when you walk through the door. He or she asks questions. What are you experiencing? When did it start? Has anything changed? Where does it hurt? Then there may be bloodwork, imaging, or other tests. The symptoms matter, but they are the beginning of the investigation, not the conclusion.

Only after gathering enough information does the doctor determine what may be causing the symptoms and decide what to do about it.

Organizations don't always give themselves the same benefit.

The Pressure to Fix Something

When an organizational result isn't what leadership expected, there is understandable pressure to act.

Engagement scores fall, so leadership launches an engagement initiative. Turnover increases, so the organization introduces a retention program. Collaboration is poor, so teams are sent to training. Work takes too long, so a new technology platform is purchased. Performance declines, so the organization restructures.

Any one of those responses might ultimately be appropriate.

The problem is that the solution is often selected before anyone has established what is actually producing the result.

Part of the reason is that action feels productive. Diagnosing can feel slow. Leaders are expected to make decisions, solve problems, and show progress. Saying, "We don't know enough yet" can feel uncomfortable when employees, boards, customers, or other stakeholders are waiting for something to change.

But speed at the beginning can become expensive later.

A new system will not fix unclear decision authority. Training will not solve a process that makes the desired behavior difficult. A reorganization will not eliminate problems rooted in how information moves or how decisions are made. An engagement initiative will not resolve the conditions that caused people to disengage.

The prescription may be perfectly good.

It may simply be treating the wrong condition.

A Symptom Is Information, Not a Diagnosis

A headache can have dozens of causes. Dehydration. Eyestrain. Stress. An infection. Medication. Lack of sleep. Something much more serious.

The existence of the headache tells the physician something is happening. It doesn't tell the physician what is causing it.

Organizational symptoms work much the same way.

High turnover tells you people are leaving. It doesn't tell you why.

Missed deadlines tell you work isn't being completed when expected. They don't tell you whether the cause is workload, competing priorities, unclear ownership, unnecessary approvals, insufficient capability, poor coordination, or something else entirely.

Low engagement tells you something about the employee experience. It doesn't tell you what created that experience.

Customer complaints, declining productivity, recurring conflict, slow decisions, inconsistent performance, and failed initiatives all provide useful information. But each is a presenting complaint. There is still work to do before deciding what it means.

That distinction sounds simple. In practice, it changes the questions an organization asks.

Instead of beginning with, "How do we improve engagement?" the question becomes, "What is producing the engagement levels we're seeing?"

Instead of, "How do we reduce turnover?" it becomes, "What is producing turnover here, and where is it actually occurring?"

Instead of, "How do we get managers to communicate better?" it becomes, "What is happening in the organization that makes communication inconsistent?"

Those questions may eventually lead to an engagement initiative, a retention strategy, or management training.

They may also lead somewhere nobody expected.

Sometimes the First Explanation Is the Wrong One

This is where diagnosis becomes particularly important.

Suppose an organization has unusually high turnover in one division. The immediate explanation might be compensation. Leadership conducts a market analysis, adjusts salaries, and waits for retention to improve.

But what if compensation wasn't producing the turnover?

What if employees were leaving because decisions routinely changed without explanation? Or because one manager had become a bottleneck for advancement? Or because workloads were distributed unevenly? Or because people saw no future for themselves in the organization?

A compensation adjustment may still have been worthwhile. It just wasn't a treatment for the problem leadership thought it was treating.

The same thing happens when organizations respond to recurring performance issues with training. Training makes sense when people lack knowledge or capability. It makes far less sense when employees already know what to do but organizational systems make it difficult to do it.

Before asking what intervention to buy, build, launch, or implement, it is worth establishing whether the intervention addresses the condition that is actually producing the outcome.

Diagnosis Changes the Starting Point

This is the work I do with organizations.

Before recommending a solution, I ask questions. I look at data. I talk to people experiencing the organization from different vantage points. I look for patterns across what leadership believes is happening, what employees describe, what the systems require, and what the results show.

Sometimes those things tell the same story.

Sometimes they don't.

That difference matters because the presenting problem is not always the actual problem.

An organization may believe it has a communication problem when it has a decision-making problem. What appears to be resistance to change may be the predictable response to a change employees don't understand or don't believe will last. A performance problem may turn out to be a process problem. A collaboration problem may have less to do with relationships than with competing incentives that make collaboration irrational.

You cannot know which one you're dealing with simply by looking at the symptom.

You have to diagnose it.

Before the Next Prescription

There will always be pressure to move quickly when something isn't working. Sometimes speed is necessary.

But there is a difference between moving quickly and moving prematurely.

The next time an organizational result causes concern, resist the temptation to begin with, "What should we do about this?"

Start one question earlier.

What is actually producing this outcome?

That question may take you somewhere different from where you expected to go. It may challenge the explanation everyone has already accepted. It may reveal that the solution being discussed has very little to do with the problem underneath it.

And sometimes it may confirm that the solution you were considering was right all along.

Either way, now you know why you're prescribing it.

What would change if your organization diagnosed the problem before reaching for the next fix?
